article.overview: A lunar optical interferometer is an instrument that combines light collected by two or more separated telescopes so that the combined measurement reveals much finer angular detail than either telescope could resolve alone. The payloads in this group are concepts rather than flown instruments. MoonLITE is a NASA Astrophysics Pioneers proposal to fly a two-telescope visible-light interferometer on a commercial lunar lander, with one telescope on the lander and a second placed about 100 metres away by a rover [1]. Artemis-enabled Stellar Imager (AeSI) is a NASA-linked NIAC concept for a larger ultraviolet and optical interferometer array on the lunar surface [2]. Neither source shows that these concepts have been selected, funded or scheduled for launch.
article.description: An optical interferometer measures the interference pattern produced when light from two apertures is brought together. The spacing between the apertures, called the baseline, determines the finest detail the instrument can measure. A baseline of 100 metres is far larger than any single telescope aperture that could be carried on a lander, so the angular resolution of the combined system can be far higher than that of either telescope alone [1]. On the Moon, the two telescopes would be placed on the surface rather than flown on separate spacecraft. This is the central design idea behind both concepts. Surface placement avoids the need for spacecraft to hold their relative positions in orbit, because the telescopes sit on the ground and gravity keeps them in place [1]. The concepts therefore trade the complexity of free-flying formation control for the logistics of landing and deploying hardware on the surface. The payload described here is a class of instrument rather than one design. The two concepts discussed below differ greatly in scale, wavelength coverage and maturity, and their figures must not be compared directly.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of an optical interferometer is to see fine angular structure in astronomical objects that is invisible to single telescopes of practical size. The sources describe several target classes. Measuring the angular sizes of very cool stars and substellar objects, including the smallest and coolest exoplanet host stars, is a MoonLITE goal [1]. Searching for close stellar companions around exoplanet-hosting stars is also a MoonLITE goal [1]. The AeSI concept aims to resolve the surfaces of stars and their magnetic activity, and to examine inner accretion disks around young stars and black holes [2]. Extragalactic work, including the inner regions of active galactic nucleus jets, is illustrated in the MoonLITE paper with radio interferometry examples [1]. Longer-term AeSI goals include imaging surface features and weather on nearby exoplanets [2]. MoonLITE plans a guest observer programme [1].
article.operating_principle: In a separated-aperture interferometer, light from each telescope is transported to a common beam combiner. The combiner brings the two beams together so that they interfere, and the resulting fringe pattern is recorded. The contrast and phase of the fringes encode the angular structure of the observed source. In the MoonLITE design, each feed station includes an articulating siderostat that feeds a fixed 50 mm refractor, and light from the outboard station is carried to the main instrument by polarisation-maintaining single-mode optical fibre through an umbilical cable. Light shorter than 620 nm is split off by a dichroic and sent to a fine-guidance CCD camera, while longer wavelengths go into the fibre. The beam combiner uses a polarisation-based quadrature extraction architecture described as similar to the VLTI PRIMA instrument [1]. The AeSI concept is described as a long-baseline ultraviolet and optical imaging interferometer. The primary sources reviewed here do not give its optical design in detail [2].
article.scientific_importance: The sources argue that the Moon offers a stable platform for interferometry. The Surveyor 3 probe and the Apollo 12 lunar module descent stage have remained about 180 metres apart for roughly 50 years, with their relative position staying static at the sub-micron level [1]. A lunar telescope has also operated for a long period. The Chang'e-3 lander's Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope reported more than 1.5 years of highly stable operation on the lunar surface [1]. These examples support the idea that a surface instrument can hold its alignment over long periods, but they do not prove that a two-telescope interferometer will perform as predicted.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for an optical interferometer. The values below describe two specific concepts. Only numbers stated in the sources are given; missing values are null and marked as not stated.

examples.name: MoonLITE (proposed NASA Astrophysics Pioneers mission)
examples.type: Proposed lunar surface optical interferometer (proposal stage, 2024)
examples.aperture_description: Two 5 cm apertures; each feed station includes an articulating siderostat feeding a fixed 50 mm refractor, as stated in the MoonLITE paper.
examples.wavelength_band: Visible. Light below 620 nm is split off to a fine-guidance CCD; the paper gives no further band edges.
examples.sensitivity_basis: Estimate for isolated objects. Baseline requirement is a 300 s exposure with a goal of 3000 s. Assumes 2 electron read noise, 70 percent detector quantum efficiency, 98.5 percent mirror reflectivity over 30 reflections and 1 to 4 dB/km fibre attenuation.
examples.resolution_targets: Stated targets, not achieved measurements: measurements down to 0.4 to 1.4 milliarcseconds with errors below 0.1 percent; angular sizes down to 100 microarcseconds with errors below 10 percent. The paper also claims a 6 to 7 magnitude sensitivity gain over current ground-based direct fringe sensing limits.
examples.power_and_comms_note: The umbilical carries electrical power and communications fed by the lander. No power or data-rate figure is stated.
examples.qualification: Proposal-stage concept. Laboratory test setup is 300 mm by 450 mm and has not been optimised for size or weight, so it is not a flight dimension. Selection, funding and launch status not verified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Artemis-enabled Stellar Imager (AeSI) concept
examples.type: Proposed NIAC lunar UV and optical long-baseline imaging interferometer (feasibility study)
examples.wavelength_band: Visible and ultraviolet, described qualitatively; no numeric range stated.
examples.sensitivity_and_resolution: No numeric resolution or sensitivity figure stated in the sources reviewed.
examples.qualification: Feasibility concept under NIAC Phase 1 (began April 2024). The 15-telescope, 30-telescope expansion and 1 km major axis figures come only from search-indexed summaries of the NASA-linked Phase 1 work and have not been verified against the primary report, which could not be retrieved. The NASA project page returned a 404 error and the repository record returned HTTP 400.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No dimensions are verified for either concept. The MoonLITE laboratory test setup is 300 mm by 450 mm, but it is an engineering development bench setup, not a flight configuration. The AeSI reference array geometry (an elliptical array) is reported only in unverified summaries.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass figure is verified for MoonLITE or AeSI. The MoonLITE paper does not state an instrument mass, and the AeSI paper does not state one either. A 2024 Pioneers CLPS allocation of 50 kg reported in a secondary summary is not verified and is not used here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No power figure is verified for MoonLITE or AeSI. The MoonLITE umbilical carries power and communications fed by the lander, with no figure stated. A 200 W Pioneers allocation reported in a secondary summary is not verified and is not used here.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The Moon has no substantial atmosphere, so an optical telescope on the surface avoids the atmospheric turbulence that limits ground-based observations. The surface, however, experiences a long lunar day and night and extreme temperature swings. The MoonLITE paper states that nighttime operations are likely not an option in the near future because extreme cold limits battery life. The baseline plan is two lunar days of science operations, with roughly 300 hours of observing in each day, and CLPS survival over at least one non-operational night with a goal of up to six such cycles [1]. Dust is a significant concern. The paper describes lunar dust as abrasive, with glass-shard particles that can rapidly degrade unprotected mechanical devices. A siderostat design that protects the optics from dust levitated during sunrise and sunset is presented as essential [1]. Sky coverage is constrained by the Moon's rotation, which is about 28 times slower than Earth's, leaving many hours of clock time for observing. The paper notes that lunar libration of about 6.7 degrees is not modelled in its coverage plot [1].
article.limitations: Both concepts are early-stage. MoonLITE is described as a proposal and AeSI as a feasibility study. Neither has a flight design, mission manifest or confirmed lander interface in the sources reviewed. The sensitivity and resolution figures for MoonLITE are estimates that depend on stated assumptions, not measured performance. The paper's abstract refers to gains of many magnitudes over ground-based interferometry, while its body text gives 6 to 7 magnitudes. Night operations are limited, and the dust and thermal problems described above have not been demonstrated for a lunar interferometer.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface optical interferometer would be delivered to the Moon as part of a commercial lunar lander mission or a larger surface payload. For MoonLITE, the CLPS lander would carry the inboard telescope and a CLPS rover would carry the pre-loaded outboard telescope.
transportation_process: Integrate the inboard station on a CLPS-provided lander and the outboard station on a CLPS-provided rover; integration details are not verified in the sources reviewed.
Launch and transfer to the Moon on the CLPS delivery vehicle; the MoonLITE paper does not describe launch or transfer parameters.
Land the lander with the inboard telescope on the lunar surface.
Drive the rover about 100 metres from the lander while paying out the umbilical cable that carries light and electrical power and communications.
Set down the outboard station, calibrate, then begin science operations. Science is planned for two lunar days with about 300 hours of observing in each day.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: MoonLITE uses a rover to place the outboard station about 100 metres from the lander in a single deployment, paying out a fibre-and-power umbilical. The AeSI deployment method is not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope reported more than 1.5 years of highly stable operation on the lunar surface and is cited as surface-instrument precedent. The Surveyor 3 and Apollo 12 descent stage pairing has remained about 180 metres apart for roughly 50 years.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander or rover is verified. The MoonLITE paper names a CLPS-provided lander and rover but does not give verified interface specifications for power, data, thermal control, mass or landing loads, and no lander compatibility is asserted here.

article.historical_significance: The concept of a lunar interferometer is recent. A 1996 study favoured free-flying interferometers because the Moon then lacked the infrastructure to support a surface observatory. The 2024 MoonLITE and AeSI proposals mark a shift in that reasoning, because Artemis-era infrastructure could make surface siting more practical [2]. MoonLITE uses the Surveyor 3 and Apollo 12 pairing as evidence that surface hardware can stay aligned for decades [1]. The Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope is cited as a surface-instrument precedent [1].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Status: MoonLITE is a 2024 proposal. A search for selection, funding or launch status in 2025 and 2026 did not find a confirmation. The current status must be checked against NASA Astrophysics Pioneers or CLPS announcements. Performance figures for MoonLITE are estimates and stated targets, not measurements, and the paper's many-magnitudes abstract wording is inconsistent with its 6 to 7 magnitude body text. A 110 microarcsecond resolution figure appears in secondary search summaries but not in the MoonLITE paper text reviewed, so it is not used. AeSI has only qualitative wavelength information and no verified numeric performance, mass or power. Its 15-telescope, 30-telescope and 1 km array figures are unverified. No AeSI image was verified from an official page.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Image URLs were taken from the figure src attributes of the MoonLITE arXiv HTML page; they were not downloaded.

data_quality_notes: MoonLITE is a 2024 proposal. Selection, funding and launch status were not confirmed by searches run for 2025 and 2026. The current status must be checked against NASA Astrophysics Pioneers or CLPS announcements.
MoonLITE sensitivity (visual magnitude 17) and resolution targets are estimates and goals stated by the authors, not achieved measurements.
The MoonLITE paper abstract says many magnitudes over ground-based interferometry; its section 5 says 6 to 7 magnitudes. The body text figure is used.
A 110 microarcsecond resolution figure appears in secondary search summaries of MoonLITE but not in the paper text that was reviewed. It is not used in the article.

A 2024 Pioneers CLPS allocation of 50 kg, 200 W and 300 kbps with daytime-only operations appears only in a secondary search summary of a presentation. It is not verified and is not used in the article.

AeSI reference design figures (15 telescopes, expandable to 30, elliptical array with a 1 km major axis) appear only in search-indexed summaries. The NASA project page returned a 404 error and the NIAC Phase 1 repository record returned HTTP 400. They are flagged as unverified in the article and JSON.
The AeSI Phase 1 report is said to have been delivered in March 2025 with a Phase 2 recommendation, but this comes from a secondary summary and was not verified. The Phase 2 status is unknown.
No AeSI-specific image was verified from an official source, so no AeSI image is included.

Image URLs were taken from the arXiv HTML figure src attributes (no query strings) and were not downloaded or resolution-checked. The Surveyor 3 photograph is a NASA image reproduced in an arXiv paper; its reuse rights should be checked against NASA image policy.
Site and landing location recommendations, which the AeSI paper discusses, are excluded per the brief.
